body.hook: Investors hear hundreds of pitches. Most are forgotten within minutes. The ones that win explain a real problem, a clear solution and why it matters, in about two minutes. Today you learn to pitch.

study.title: Pitch Builder
study.question: How do I persuade people that my product is worth it?
study.passage:
Pitch structure (written for this lesson), about two minutes:
1. Hook (10 s): a surprising fact or question from your research. "60% of students we surveyed miss homework deadlines at least sometimes."
2. Problem (20 s): your problem statement and a user story.
3. Solution (30 s): what your product does, shown in a demo or images.
4. Value proposition (15 s): "Our app helps student athletes never miss a deadline by showing tomorrow's homework in one tap."
5. Evidence (20 s): user-test results, such as "task success rose from 40% to 100%."
6. Competitors (10 s): why yours is different or better.
7. Call to action (10 s): what you want: "Try it this week" or "Help us launch it school-wide."
Value proposition formula: Our [product] helps [target market] [do something] by [how it works].

body.objective: Students will be able to present to a panel.

body.hook: On shows like Dragons' Den, entrepreneurs pitch to a panel who fire tough questions: How much does it cost? Who will buy it? What if it breaks? Today you face your own panel.

vocabulary.definition: A group of people who listen to and judge pitches.

study.title: Pitch Panel
study.question: How do I handle a panel's questions with confidence?
study.passage:
Pitch panel format (written for this lesson):
Each team pitches for two minutes, then the panel (classmates, teachers or invited guests) asks questions for three minutes.
Common panel questions: "Who exactly will use this?" "How do you know they want it?" "What does it cost to make or run?" "What if users stop using it after a week?" "How is it better than what already exists?" "What would you do with more time or money?"
Answering tips: pause before answering; use evidence ("In our testing, 4 of 5 users..."); admit what you don't know and say how you'd find out; stay respectful even if the question feels tough.
Panel scoring (1–4 each): problem is real and clear; solution fits the problem; evidence supports claims; delivery is confident; answers to questions are thoughtful.
After the panel: list the three most useful questions and your next steps.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Prepare answers to the six common questions
Deliver your pitch to the panel

discussion: Which question was hardest to answer?

body.objective: Students will be able to plan high school CTS courses.
body.iCan: I can plan high school CTS courses.
successCriteria: I can describe how CTS works in Alberta high schools
I can connect my CTF experiences to CTS courses
I can make a high school course plan that fits my interests
body.hook: In Grade 10, CTF becomes CTS: Career and Technology Studies. Instead of trying a little of everything, you choose courses in areas like cooking, construction, computer science, fashion, media or health, and they count toward your high school diploma. Planning now helps you choose wisely.

vocabulary.definition: Alberta's high school program of hands-on courses that build career skills.
A unit earned for completing a high school course; Alberta's high school diploma needs at least 100.
A planned series of courses leading toward a goal.
The three CTS levels, from beginner to more specialized.
A program where high school students earn credits toward both high school and a post-secondary certificate.
Education after high school, such as college, polytechnic, apprenticeship or university.

study.title: My Pathway Plan
study.question: How can CTS courses help me explore careers in high school?
study.passage:
Information (summary written for this lesson):
CTS courses are organized in the same five clusters as CTF: Business, Finance and Information Technology; Health, Recreation and Human Services; Media, Design and Communication Arts; Natural Resources; and Trades, Manufacturing and Transportation.
Courses come in introductory, intermediate and advanced levels, and each CTS course is usually worth 1 credit. Students can build a pathway, for example Foods: introductory foods courses in Grade 10 leading to advanced courses in Grade 12.
Related programs: RAP (start an apprenticeship in high school), dual credit (earn college credits) and work experience.
Case studies: Leila loved the CTF foods challenge and plans foods courses each year, plus work experience at a bakery. Marcus liked coding his CTF app and plans computer science courses and a dual-credit program. Aisha enjoyed building her organizer and plans construction courses and RAP as a carpentry apprentice.
Task: Use your CTF portfolio and interest results to plan a CTS pathway for Grades 10–12.
study.source: Summary written for this lesson; check your school's course guide and Alberta Education information for current CTS courses.

Add a related program and a possible career goal
